newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Tactical voting in NZ - it's simple, isn't it?.
newsitem.headline: Tactical voting in NZ - it's simple, isn't it?.

text.p: New Zealand's new mixed member proportional system was intended to allow people to pick their party of choice rather than the former first-past-the-post system where often it was the lesser of two evils, right?

In the close contest in Wellington Central -- considered the most crucial of the 65 electoral seats -- the tactical voting book has been re-written so your enemy's enemy is your friend and your ally's ally may be your enemy.

The seat is seen as pivotal because if Act New Zealand leader Richard Prebble wins, his free market party, an ally of the ruling, but struggling National Party, will win its share of seats without having to cross a five percent threshold nationwide.

Sarah Porter of the nationalist New Zealand First Party has told her supporters to vote for conservative National candidate Mark Thomas or Labour's Alick Shaw -- NZ First's potential coalition partners -- in order to keep out Prebble.
Labour voters are in two minds in their backing for Shaw. Many are contemplating voting for National's Thomas in order to stop Prebble so that National will be left without a coalition partner.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger on Thursday predicted Prebble would win the seat, interpreted by the media as either a hint to vote for Prebble or an attempt to stop tactical voting elsewhere for Act which would eat into National's countrywide vote.
Then there is the left-wing Alliance.

It has ruled out a coation after the election but its voters are also in two minds whether to back Shaw, to keep both conservative candidates out, or to vote for Thomas to stop Prebble and thereby stop a National-led government so the Alliance can back a Labour-led government without actually being part of it.
